Well, if you have a full chroot you can just do "--mount-bind /some/chroot /" and you don't have to create much files. However, for xdg-app I _want_ to have an internal tmpfs, because it is guaranteed to be isolated from the host, and cleaned up by the kernel when its not in use anymore.

It may make sense to expose some container /tmp to systemd-tmpfiles, but I don't think that is a always what you want.

If the host /tmp is not a tmpfs you can't pivot_root at all from it, so i don't think relying on that is a good idea. What is the problem with using a tmpfs?
That is kind of hard to use though. Especially from the shell. I think we could have a set of pre-build BPF sets linked into the app, and then be able to pass via an FD for additional rules.
Well, we have to be _some_ gid at least, how would we pick that? We could leave any extra groups though.
You can't call setenv() in the parent, because execing a setuid helper clears LD_LIBRARY_PATH. However, yes, a --setenv would work too.
I was thinking `--drop-groups` would just use the default gid from `struct passwd`.

This is just about trying to reduce the amount of setuid code - if we can figure out how to have the caller create the files, a _lot_ of things drop out.

Maybe we have `--rootfs-prepare /usr/bin/mysandbox-rootfs-prep` which gets called with its cwd pointing to the tmpfs, but using the host's mount namespace?

The way I'm thinking of this is - the tool shouldn't have any more than we would want in the kernel.  We wouldn't put generating `/etc/passwd` files into the kernel, so this tool shouldn't do it either.
Keep in mind I see the goal here as to define a core - a higher level tool can add lots of porcelain that runs without any privileges.

Can you bind-mount a /proc/self/fd file? If so you could pass in e.g. the passwd files as a fd and bind mount that. 

I would very much like to keep everything related to a container owned by the container so that its auto-cleaned-up by the kernel. This is very important in the desktop case where things are started ad-hoc and there is no tracking of "all running containers" by some management thing.

I thougth initially about allowing the caller to shell out before the final unmount of the host fs, but its tricky. You have to create things in the right order, and you likely will need a mix of file creation and bind mounts, so you'll need to allow shelling out at arbitrary points in the construction of the root.

In the end I was not able to make that work though, because for it to work it has to happen before the pivot_root so that the host side binaries work. But in that case --bind-mount / / does not work, because that would try to bind-mount / onto something inside / which fails the mount. For that to work i had to make the tmpfs root the real root, and then pivot_root so that both the new root and the old root are subdirs of the in-between root.

True.

What about security issues though. Does the kernel verify the passed in BPF? Are there any risks with loading arbitrary bits as a seccomp ruleset?

Not any more than there are without this tool.  There's nothing special about libseccomp - it's just a userspace library for making them, any userspace today can access the seccomp system call and install whatever it wants.

https://lwn.net/Articles/656307/
What we could do is traditional privilege separation though. I.e. fork and drop caps for all but the operations that need caps.

This branch is an experiment with privilege separation:
https://github.com/alexlarsson/bubblewrap/tree/privilege-separation

Yeah, i want to move that out to a generic "pull data from fd", but it still seems like a worthwile thing.

The reason I'm concerned about this is - while because we're using the user's uid as the fsuid, most filesystem operations should be pretty safe, I have a lingering concern about a stray portion of a synthetic fs (cgroup, proc, sysfs) that has DAC permissions that allow a user to read/write to it but gates on CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the code.

I briefly looked at:

```
for x in /proc /sys; do
  find $x -type f -uid 0 -perm -o+w 2>/dev/null
done
```

There is one in the cgroup code that looks safe, some selinux things that also look safe (they require the requisite selinux perms) but `/proc/$pid/attr` jumped out as writable.  Luckily, writing to these requires `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, not `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.  But still...
Yeah, but with the privilege-separation in the above branch we would not touch these files as CAP_SYSADMIN. Only the mounts happen with privileges.

OK, right.  I'd still feel more comfortable if we moved as much as possible out of the binary.  We could have `bwrap-core` which is setuid, and install a `bwrap-cli` which is a friendlier (unprivileged) wrapper?

This would be up to the policy writer.  But the bottom line would be we need to either allow unconfined_t to transition to --exec-label, or unconfined_t @bwrap_exec_t -> bwrap_t,  And then bwrap_t would need to be able to transition to the label specified by the user.
